claims.text: A conventional low-alloy steel susceptible to temper embrittlement can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition through thermal treatment.
The proposed starting material is a conventionally processed low-alloy steel with known susceptibility to temper embrittlement.
Entering a narrow temper-embrittlement temperature window will cause the steel to become brittle.
Further cooling or heating to leave the embrittlement window will restore ductility.
Impurity segregation promotes embrittlement in the intermediate thermal state.
A subsequent temperature regime alleviates impurity segregation and restores ductility.
The relevant structural mediator is the degree of phosphorus or other embrittling-element segregation at grain boundaries.
At intermediate temperatures, impurities segregate to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation causes a loss of ductility.
Further temperature change alters impurity-segregation kinetics or solubility.
Altered segregation kinetics or solubility re-establishes a ductile state.
The steel will be ductile at high temperatures, brittle over a narrow intermediate temperature range, and ductile again outside that range.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys consistently exhibit high ductility.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys do not exhibit temper embrittlement.
The proposed transition occurs only within a specific narrow temperature window governed by impurity-segregation kinetics in conventional low-alloy steels.
The transition may not be reproducible in alloys with substantially different compositions or impurity levels.
